blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A two-tailed test looks for a difference from H₀ in either direction (H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0). A one-tailed test looks in one pre-specified direction only (H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ > 0, or < 0).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The direction in H₁ (recall §8.2) decides where the rejection region sits. A two-tailed test splits α between the two tails: α/2 = 0.025 in each at α = 0.05. A one-tailed test puts all of α in one tail. That makes it easier to reject H₀ in the chosen direction, and makes the test blind to an effect in the other direction.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Urban–rural weights, z = 2.46 (§8.5).

  1. Two-tailed: critical z = ±1.96, critical difference ±1.96 × 0.406 = ±0.80 kg; p = 0.014.
  2. One-tailed (H₁: urban heavier): critical z = 1.645, critical difference 0.67 kg; p = P(Z ≥ 2.46) = 0.007, half the two-tailed value.
  3. An observed difference of 0.75 kg would be “significant” one-tailed (> 0.67) but not two-tailed (< 0.80).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A school deworming drive might change mean haemoglobin. A two-tailed test asks “is Hb different, in either direction?” A one-tailed test of “does Hb rise?” could not detect a fall, however large, because that possibility was excluded when H₁ was written.

points.html: Choose one- or two-tailed before seeing the data, on scientific grounds. Switching to one-tailed after seeing the direction halves the p-value (step 2) and is a form of p-hacking: changing the analysis until p falls below α.

Two-tailed tests are the usual default. When a one-sided hypothesis is the real question, as in a non-inferiority trial (§8.2), a one-sided test is appropriate, but say when and why it is used (Greenland et al., 2016).
For a symmetric null distribution (z or t), the two-tailed p is exactly twice the one-tailed p in the observed direction.

questions.prompt: Two studies report p = 0.001 and p = 0.049. A colleague says the first is “much more significant”, so its effect must be larger. What is right and what is wrong in this?
questions.answer: Right: both are below 0.05, and the smaller p does indicate greater incompatibility of that study’s data with H₀ under its statistical model. Wrong: (1) “significant” at α = 0.05 is a yes/no classification, and both studies cross it; (2) a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect (ASA, 2016, principle 5). A tiny effect in a very large study can give p = 0.001, and a large effect in a small study p = 0.049. To compare effects, look at each study’s effect estimate with its confidence interval.

questions.prompt: A trial tests a new drug in 8 independent subgroups, each at α = 0.05, and the drug truly does nothing. What is the probability of at least one “significant” subgroup? What per-test threshold would Bonferroni use?
questions.answer: Family-wise error rate = 1 − (1 − 0.05)⁸ = 1 − 0.95⁸ = 1 − 0.663 = 0.337: about one chance in three of a false “finding”. Bonferroni tests each subgroup at 0.05/8 = 0.00625.

questions.prompt: A district sample of 100 births has mean birthweight 2.9 kg. Test H₀: μ = 3.0 kg with σ = 0.5 kg: compute z and the two-sided p. The team, seeing the result lies below 3.0 kg, switches to a one-tailed test. What p would they report, and why is the switch wrong?
questions.answer: SE = 0.5/√100 = 0.05 kg. z = (2.9 − 3.0)/0.05 = −2.00. Two-sided p = 2 × [1 − Φ(2.00)] = 0.046. One-tailed (H₁: μ < 3.0) p = 0.023, half the two-sided value. The switch is wrong because the direction was chosen after seeing the data. It halves the p-value. A team that picks the tail the data point to, then tests at 0.05, rejects whenever the two-sided p is below 0.10, so its real Type I error rate is 10%, not the 5% it claims. This is p-hacking (§8.6). The direction must be fixed at step 1, before the data are seen. Note also that H₀ here is μ = 3.0 kg, not “no effect”.
